steps.title: Why we lock data
text: Anyone on a network wire can copy the bytes you send. If you send a secret as readable bytes, the listener reads it too.
Readable data is called {{term:plaintext}}. Scrambled data is called {{term:ciphertext}}.
{{term:aes}} is a standard lock for data. It uses a secret number, the {{term:key}}, to turn plaintext into ciphertext. Only the right key turns it back.
This lesson uses AES in three ways. Two ways hide your data well, and one way leaks patterns. Built to show the parts. Do not copy.

steps.title: One key, or a key pair
text: Locks come in two kinds. {{term:symmetric}} encryption uses one key. The same key locks the data and unlocks it, so both sides must hold a copy.
The other kind is {{term:asymmetric}}. It uses a key pair. The private key stays with its owner. The public key is safe to give to anyone, and nobody can work back from it to the private key.
A symmetric lock is fast, so it carries the data. A key pair is slow, so programs use it for small jobs: to agree on a shared key, and to prove who is talking. Lessons 3 and 4 show those jobs.
AES is a symmetric lock. This lesson is about that kind.

claims.text: Symmetric encryption uses one shared key to lock and unlock data. Asymmetric methods use a key pair: a private key that stays with its owner and a public key that anyone may hold. The private key cannot be worked out from the public key.
claims.source: NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev. 5, section 2.1, Glossary (entries: symmetric key, public key, private key, public-key (asymmetric) cryptography)

claims.text: Real protocols use the key pair to agree on a shared key and to prove identity, then lock the bulk data with a symmetric cipher.
claims.source: RFC 8446, section 2 (Protocol Overview: the handshake does key exchange and server authentication; the record protocol protects traffic with the shared keys); lesson 5 tour, L5-S01

steps.title: Both sides hold the same key
text: The client and the server now hold one 16-byte AES key. This is the symmetric case: one key, two copies.
Look at the panel named What each side knows. The Server column and the Client column each show a row named aes.key. The box at the bottom compares the two rows and says match.
No key crossed the wire here. The lab gave each side a copy. Real programs must agree on a key in public first, and lesson 3 shows how.

steps.title: The readable bytes
text: The client sends its first message. The diagram names it TextGcm1. The message is the line "Pump four is ok." four times, which is 64 bytes.
Look at the Bytes panel under the diagram. Its header says before protection, so these are the readable bytes.
Each {{term:byte}} shows as two {{term:hex}} digits. The first four bytes are 50 75 6d 70, and they spell Pump. The text at the end of each row shows the same bytes as letters.

steps.title: The scrambled bytes
text: AES locked this message in {{term:gcm}} mode. A mode is one way to use AES. GCM scrambles the data and adds a seal.
Try it: switch to the eavesdropper view. The Bytes panel then shows the 96 bytes on the wire. No letters are readable.
The field list names each part. 4 + 12 means that the part starts at byte 4 and is 12 bytes long.
The {{term:nonce}} is a number used once. The 64 scrambled bytes come next. The {{term:tag}} is a 16-byte seal that catches changes. Only the key is secret.

steps.title: Blocks, chains, and the IV
text: AES locks 16 bytes at a time. Each 16-byte piece is a {{term:block}}. A mode is the rule for a message longer than one block.
{{term:cbc}} stands for cipher block chaining. Each block is mixed with the locked block before it, so two equal blocks lock to different bytes.
The first block has nothing before it. So CBC starts with a random 16-byte {{term:iv}}, a starting value. Find the iv field in the field list. Like the nonce, the IV is not secret.

steps.title: ECB locks each block alone
text: {{term:ecb}} stands for electronic codebook. It is the simplest mode. It locks each 16-byte block alone, with no chain.
The trouble is that two equal blocks give two equal locked blocks. A picture has big patches of one color, so the pattern survives the lock.
Open the Picture tab under the diagram. Clear picture is the readable data. Locked with ECB is the scrambled bytes, drawn as dots. The outline of the pump still shows.

claims.text: ECB mode locks equal plaintext blocks to equal ciphertext blocks, so patterns in the data can show in the ciphertext.

steps.title: Count the leak
text: The server counted the repeated blocks in the locked picture. The line under the picture gives the count. The count is a measured number from the trace, and the screen invents nothing.
A good mode gives a count near zero. ECB gives a large count, and that count is the leak.
Try it: send the text message in ECB as well. No check catches it, because the lock itself works. The mode is the weak part.

tryIt.label: Send the text message in ECB

steps.title: CBC and GCM hide the shape
text: Here is the same picture locked with GCM. The locked image looks like noise, and the outline is gone.
CBC gives the same result. Check the repeat count under each picture: it stays near zero.

steps.title: GCM catches edits
text: Locking hides data. An attacker can still change the locked bytes, so GCM adds a tag that catches edits.
The server checks the tag before it trusts a message. The box named GCM tag in the diagram shows that the check passed on the normal run.
The tag shows that someone who holds the shared key made the message. Both sides hold that key, so the tag cannot say which side. A signature can, and lesson 4 shows one.
Try it: flip one bit of the locked text. The tag no longer fits, the check fails, and the server refuses the message.

tryIt.label: Flip one bit in the GCM text

claims.text: GCM decryption checks the authentication tag first and returns no plaintext when the tag check fails.

steps.title: A nonce must never repeat
text: GCM needs a new nonce for every message under one key. A repeat can let an attacker compare two messages and forge new ones.
Real GCM has no alarm for this mistake. The lab adds a box named nonce reuse detector so you can see it.
Try it: send the last message with the first nonce. The tag check still passes. Only the detector fails.

claims.text: GCM needs a nonce that is unique for each message under one key. A repeated nonce exposes the data and lets an attacker forge messages.
claims.source: NIST SP 800-38D, section 8 (Uniqueness Requirement on IVs and Keys) and Appendix A (if IVs repeat, an adversary will likely learn the hash subkey and can construct a forgery)

claims.text: The nonce reuse detector is a lab engine event. Real GCM has no built-in alarm for a repeated nonce.
claims.source: NIST SP 800-38D, Appendix A (in most cases the authenticated decryption function cannot detect an IV repetition); docs/ux-design.md, section 8, lesson 1 row (the detector is an engine event)

steps.title: Some edits slip through
text: Now flip one bit in the CBC message. No check fails, and that is the point of this step.
One block of the unlocked text turns to junk. The next block changes by that one bit, and an attacker can aim that change.
CBC hides data but cannot see edits. That is why modern designs pair a lock with a tag, as GCM does.

tryIt.label: Flip one bit in the CBC text

claims.text: In CBC, flipping one ciphertext bit garbles that block's plaintext and flips the same bit in the next block's plaintext.
claims.source: NIST SP 800-38A, section 6.2 (CBC mode); docs/lessons-1-3-names.md, Lesson 1 attacks, L1-flip-cbc

steps.title: What to take away
text: ECB hides the bytes but leaks patterns. CBC hides patterns but lets edits through. GCM hides patterns and catches edits.
Pick a mode that does both jobs, and give each message its own nonce.
AES is the symmetric lock that carries the data. Lessons 3 and 4 show the asymmetric parts that set up its key.
Built to show the parts. Do not copy.
